en: Paṭisambhidāmagga 3,
Paññāvagga 3.10.
Discourse on the Matrix (Mātikākathā)
Freedom from hunger, liberation, deliverance through knowledge, higher virtue, higher mind, higher wisdom, tranquility, knowledge, vision,
purification, renunciation, escape, seclusion, relinquishment, conduct, liberation through jhāna,
development, determination, and the holy life. [19]
“Free from hunger” means: he is free from hunger for sensual desire through renunciation; he is free from hunger for ill will through non-ill will ... pe ...
he is free from hunger for the hindrances through the first jhāna ... pe ...
he is free from hunger for all defilements through the path of arahantship.
"Liberation, liberation": one is liberated from sensual desire through renunciation;
thus it is liberation, it is release.
One is liberated from ill will through non-ill will; thus...
Liberation, release … [as before] … one is liberated from the hindrances by means of the first jhāna;
thus it is liberation, release … [as before] …
One is liberated from all defilements by means of the path of arahantship;
thus it is liberation (*mokkha*), release (*vimokkha*).
Regarding "true knowledge and liberation" (*vijjā-vimutti*): renunciation is found, thus it is true knowledge (*vijjā*); one is released from sensual desire, thus it is liberation (*vimutti*).
One who knows is liberated; one who is liberated knows—this is "liberation through knowledge" (*vijjāvimutti*).
Non-ill will is known, thus it is "knowledge"; one is liberated from ill will, thus it is "liberation."
"One who possesses clear vision is liberated; one who is liberated possesses clear vision"—thus it is "liberation through clear vision" (*vijjā-vimutti*). ... [and so on] ...
there is clear vision because the path of arahantship exists; there is liberation because one is liberated from all defilements.
One who possesses clear vision is liberated; one who is liberated possesses clear vision—this is "liberation through clear vision" (*vijjā-vimutti*).

Higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom: by means of renunciation, sensual desire is abandoned; in the sense of restraint, it is purification of virtue; in the sense of non-distraction, it is purification of mind; in the sense of seeing, it is purification of view.
The aspect of restraint therein is the training in higher virtue;
the aspect of non-distraction therein is the training in higher mind;
the aspect of vision therein is the training in higher wisdom.
Through non-ill will, there is purification of virtue in the sense of restraint from ill will...
[and so on] ...through the path of arahantship, there is purification of virtue in the sense of restraint from all defilements; there is purification of mind in the sense of non-distraction;
there is purification of view in the sense of seeing.
The aspect of restraint therein is the training in higher virtue;
the aspect of non-distraction therein is the training in higher mind;
the aspect of vision therein is the training in higher wisdom.
"Tranquility": through renunciation one allays sensual desire; through non-ill will one allays ill will ... pe ...
through the path of arahantship one allays all defilements.
"Knowledge": because sensual desire has been abandoned, renunciation is knowledge in the sense of being known.
Because ill will has been abandoned, non-ill will is knowledge in the sense of being known. ...
[and so on] ... because all defilements have been abandoned, the path of arahantship is knowledge in the sense of being known.
As for "vision": because sensual desire has been abandoned and renunciation has been seen, it is vision.
Because ill will has been abandoned, non-ill will is seen; thus it is seeing.
… [and so on] … Because all defilements have been abandoned, the path of arahantship is seen; thus it is seeing.
Regarding purification: one who abandons sensual desire is purified by renunciation.
One who abandons ill-will is purified by non-ill-will...
[and so on] ...one who abandons all defilements is purified by the path of arahantship.
"Renunciation" is the escape from sensual desires; that is to say, renunciation.
This is the escape from forms, namely, the formless.
Furthermore, whatever is become, conditioned, and dependently arisen—its cessation is the renunciation thereof.
Non-ill will is the renunciation of ill will.
For sloth and torpor, renunciation is the perception of light...
[and so on] ...for all defilements, the path of arahantship is renunciation.
As for escape: this is the escape from sensual desires, namely, renunciation.
The escape from forms is this: namely, the formless.
Furthermore, whatever is become, conditioned, and dependently arisen, its cessation is the escape.
The escape from sensual desire is renunciation.
Non-ill will is the escape from ill will...
[and so on] ...the path of arahantship is the escape from all defilements.
Solitude: renunciation is the solitude that is the escape from sensual desire... [and so on] ...
The path of arahantship is seclusion from all defilements.
"Relinquishment" means that through renunciation one relinquishes sensual desire; thus it is relinquishment.
"By means of non-ill will, one relinquishes ill will"—
this is relinquishment... [and so on] ...by means of the path of arahantship, one relinquishes all defilements— this is relinquishment.
Renunciation.
As for "conduct": one who abandons sensual desire conducts oneself with renunciation;
one who abandons ill will conducts oneself with non-ill will... [and so on].
Abandoning all defilements, one proceeds by means of the path of arahantship.
Regarding "jhāna-vimokkha": it is called *jhāna* because one meditates (*jhāyati*) upon renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
It burns away sensual desire;
thus it is "jhāna. While burning, one is liberated; thus it is "jhāna."
Meditative absorption and liberation.
Because one is liberated while meditating, it is called "jhāna-vimokkha" (meditative absorption and liberation).
They meditate, thus they are "dhammas.
They cause defilements to burn away, thus they are "jhāpaka.
One who knows both that which meditates and that which causes burning away is called a "jhāyī" (meditator).
One who meditates on jhāna.
It is called jhāna because one meditates on non-ill will;
it is called jhāna because it burns up ill will.
Jhāna is so called because it meditates; …pe… the perception of light meditates, thus it is jhāna.
It burns away sloth and torpor, thus it is *jhāna*;
... pe ... the path to arahantship burns [away defilements], thus it is *jhāna*.
It is called *jhāna* because it burns away all defilements. Thus it is *jhāna*.
"Liberated by meditating" is liberation through jhāna.
"Liberated by burning away" is...
Meditative absorption and liberation.
They are called "dhammas" because they meditate.
"They incinerate" means the defilements.
One who knows both what has been incinerated and what is being incinerated— [is called a jhāyī].
One who meditates in jhāna.
One who has perfected development is so called because, regarding development as the foundation of life, they abandon sensual desire and develop renunciation.
“He resolves the mind by means of renunciation”—
thus he is accomplished in resolution.
Being thus accomplished in development and accomplished in resolution, he lives evenly, not unevenly.
He lives rightly, not wrongly;
he lives purely, not defiled— thus he is one perfected in livelihood.
Thus, being perfected in this way in meditation, perfected in resolve, and perfected in livelihood,
whatever assembly he approaches— whether an assembly of kshatriyas, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics—
he approaches it confident and self-assured.
For what reason?
Because he is perfected in development, perfected in resolve, and perfected in livelihood.
Thinking, "Abandoning ill will, I develop non-ill will,"...
One perfected in development … [as before] … abandoning sloth and torpor, develops the perception of light—
thus one is perfected in development … [as before] …
"Abandoning restlessness, he develops non-distraction"—
thus he is accomplished in development …pe… "Abandoning doubt, he develops the definition of phenomena"— thus he is accomplished in development.
One accomplished in development ... [as before] ...
abandoning ignorance, one develops true knowledge—thus one is accomplished in development ... [as before] ...
"Abandoning discontent, he develops gladness"—
this is one perfected in development.
…pe… "Abandoning the hindrances, he develops the first jhāna"— this is one perfected in development.
One perfected in development ... [as before] ...
abandoning all defilements, develops the path to arahantship;
thus, one is "perfected in development."
One resolves the mind by means of the path of arahantship;
thus, one is accomplished in resolution.
Being thus accomplished in development and accomplished in resolution, one lives evenly, not unevenly.
He lives rightly, not wrongly;
he lives purely, not defiled— thus he is one perfected in livelihood.
One who is thus perfected in meditation, perfected in resolve, and perfected in livelihood,
whatever assembly he approaches— whether an assembly of kshatriyas, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics—
he approaches confident and self-assured.
For what reason?
Because he is perfected in development, perfected in resolve, and perfected in livelihood.
The Discourse on the Schedule is finished.
The third chapter is the Chapter on Wisdom (Paññāvagga).
Its summary verse is:
Wisdom, supernormal power, and realization.
Seclusion and conduct as the fifth;
the miracle, the even-headedness,
the foundations of mindfulness, and insight.
In the third chapter on wisdom,
there are ten in the matrix;
the Great Chapter is the Coupling.
And the Paññāvagga by name;
these are the three chapters in this Paṭisambhidāpakaraṇa.
In the paths of infinite principles,
he is deep like the ocean;
like the sky studded with stars, he is vast.
Like a large, deep lake,
it is the illumination of knowledge for yogis who are like storytellers at a vast assembly.
The Pāḷi of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* is finished.
